🧙‍♂️🕷️ Lord of the Rings Session #5 - Frodo, Sam, Gollum, and the burden getting uglier

Book-club discussion - The Two Towers, Book IV.

Short summary

Last session stayed with the war side of The Two Towers. This one goes back to the smaller, lonelier, more spiritually dangerous road. Frodo. Sam. Gollum. Hunger. Swamps. Stairs. Trust. Pity. Exhaustion. The Ring getting heavier in a way that is not just physical. This is the part of Tolkien where the adventure gets less grand and more intimate. No armies to hide behind. No heroic speeches to make the burden noble. Just three figures moving through a poisoned landscape, and the uncomfortable question of what mercy costs when the person you pity might still betray you.

Reading for this session

The Two Towers - Book IV

From The Taming of Sméagol through The Choices of Master Samwise.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “Is Gollum pitiable, dangerous, funny, tragic, or all of those at once?”
• “Does Frodo trust Gollum, use him, pity him, or need him?”
• “What makes Sam’s loyalty beautiful, and where does it become limited?”
• “Why does this section feel so much lonelier than the war chapters?”
• “What does Tolkien understand about addiction, burden, and divided selves?”
• “By the end, who understands the Ring best?”

We’ll start with one question: “What image from this section stayed with you?” Then I’ll do a quick map reset and we’ll stay close to the scenes and choices. Not lore-flexing. Not pronunciation Olympics. Not book-report voice. A real Tolkien room.

events.description:
👁️ Debate Night - should you be your real self in public, or put on a mask?

Structured debate + room vote.

Short summary

Visibility sounds like freedom. Be recognized. Be represented. Stop hiding. That is the good version. But there is another version too: being watched, branded, judged, flattened, disciplined, and turned into a public identity before you have even had time to be a person. So here is the motion: Being more visible makes people freer. You will have to take a side. This debate is tied to shame, freedom, public identity, social media, Pride, self-consciousness, and whether being out in the open liberates people or trains them to perform themselves better. Not culture-war sludge. Not slogans. A real debate.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• "When does visibility become freedom, and when does it become surveillance?"
• "Can being out in the open reduce shame, or does it create new kinds of performance?"
• "Does public identity protect people, or trap them inside a simpler version of themselves?"
• "What has social media done to the feeling of being watched?"
• "Is privacy still necessary for becoming yourself?"
• "Who benefits when everyone is encouraged to be more visible?"

Optional fuel for the debate

• TED - Glenn Greenwald: Why privacy matters
• TED - Monica Lewinsky: The price of shame
• Pew Research Center - Americans and Privacy

How the debate will work

We'll start with a quick vote: Yes / No / Undecided. Then we split the room by current lean and debate the strongest version of both sides. Short comments beat speeches. Strong arguments beat loud certainty. Changing your mind is allowed. No dunking. No dominance games. No turning identity into a weapon. A serious room.

events.description:
🔥🚁 Apocalypse Now - war, madness, spectacle, and the end of command

Movie discussion - watch beforehand. No screening.

Short summary

Some movies are about war. Apocalypse Now feels more like war having a fever dream about itself. It is huge, beautiful, obscene, hypnotic, ridiculous, and rotten in a way that still makes most modern war movies look too clean. This is not just a Vietnam film. It is about command breaking down, spectacle replacing meaning, violence turning mystical, men losing the ability to tell the difference between mission and madness. That is why it still deserves a room. Not because it is “important cinema.” Because it is still disturbing. A movie this visually powerful should make us suspicious of our own attention.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “Is the movie condemning spectacle, or seducing us with it?”
• “At what point does the mission stop making sense?”
• “Is Kurtz insane, honest, monstrous, or just what the war was already becoming?”
• “What does the film understand about command and masculinity?”
• “Which scene felt most impossible to forget?”
• “Does the movie have a moral center, or is that exactly what has collapsed?”

How the afternoon will go

Come having watched the film beforehand. We’ll start with one question: “What scene still feels lodged in your nervous system?” Then we’ll stay close to the film: Willard, Kurtz, the river, the helicopters, the spectacle, the horror, and the feeling that order has become a costume. Not trivia. Not film-bro monologues. Not war-movie ranking night. A real discussion.

events.description:
VIFF movie outing - public screening, optional short chat after.

Short summary

A lot of animated films ask you to choose a side. Princess Mononoke does something more grown-up and more painful. The forest is not innocent. Industry is not simply evil. The gods are terrifying. The humans are desperate. Everyone is wounded, hungry, proud, and half-right. That is what makes this one of Miyazaki’s greatest films. It is not a clean environmental fable. It is a war between ways of living, and the movie refuses to let anyone escape with a simple moral slogan. This is the kind of film that deserves a room: beautiful, furious, mythic, political, and still hard to reduce.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “Who is the film most sympathetic to, and does that change as you watch?”
• “Is coexistence actually possible here, or just the least impossible hope?”
• “What does the film understand about rage?”
• “Are the gods sacred, monstrous, or both?”
• “Does Lady Eboshi feel like a villain, a realist, a builder, or all three?”
• “Why does this movie make every easy answer feel dishonest?”

How the evening will go

We’ll meet at VIFF Centre before the screening, watch the film together, and whoever still has energy can stay for a short chat after. This is a public VIFF screening, not a private Meetup event. Please buy your own VIFF ticket while available.

events.description:
VIFF movie outing - public screening, optional short chat after.

Short summary

It is very easy to be smug about Titanic. Too famous. Too big. Too romantic. Too many people have already cried over the door. And yet. The movie still works. Partly because James Cameron understands spectacle. Partly because the romance is built with embarrassing confidence. Partly because the class story is not subtle but still lands. And partly because the whole film is really about memory: an old woman telling the story of the moment when her life split in two. That is what makes this worth seeing with people. Not ironic nostalgia. Not “is there room on the door?” discourse for two hours. A real conversation about sincerity, disaster, class, image, memory, and why some massive popular movies survive the jokes made about them.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “Why does Titanic still work, even after all the parody?”
• “Is the romance simple, or exactly as simple as it needs to be?”
• “What does the film understand about class without being subtle about it?”
• “Does the spectacle deepen the emotion, or overpower it?”
• “Why does Rose’s memory frame matter so much?”
• “Is this a great film, a great popular film, or are those the same thing sometimes?”

events.description:
VIFF movie outing - public screening, optional short chat after.

Short summary

A lot of sci-fi ages into nostalgia. The Matrix aged into an accusation. Yes, it still has the coats, the bullet time, the sunglasses, the style. But what keeps it alive is the uglier thing underneath all that coolness: how much of your life is actually yours, and how much of it was handed to you so smoothly you stopped noticing? Reality. Simulation. Bodies. Control. Choice. Comfort. The strange appeal of waking up, and the cost of not being able to go back to sleep. This movie rewired how people talk about the world. That is rare. I want the real discussion, not internet red-pill sludge and not trivia about bullet time.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “Would you really want the truth if it ruined your life?”
• “Is the Matrix mainly about freedom, control, or the desire to feel chosen?”
• “Was Cypher weak, honest, or saying something most people quietly feel?”
• “What part of the film stopped feeling futuristic and started feeling familiar?”
• “Do people want reality, or just a more flattering simulation?”
• “Once you wake up, are you free, or just trapped in a harsher system?”

How the evening will go

We’ll meet at VIFF Centre before the screening, watch the film together, and whoever wants can stay for a short post-film chat. This is a public VIFF screening, not a private Meetup event. Please buy your own VIFF ticket while available.

🪞⚖️ Do Looks Matter More Than We Admit?

Debate / discussion session — watch beforehand if you can, or read the shorter summary.

Short summary

Everyone says looks should not matter. Then dating apps exist. Hiring bias exists. Social warmth exists. Attention exists. Strangers treat people differently before a word has been said. That is the uncomfortable starting point for this discussion. The anchor is the conversation between Dr. Mikhail Varshavski, better known as Doctor Mike, and Dr. Mike Israetel on *The Checkup with Doctor Mike*: The Science Of Being “Ugly.” The conversation moves through attractiveness, dating apps, confidence, cosmetic surgery, body change, cultural norms, vanity, health, and the awkward question of whether pretending looks do not matter actually helps anyone. Two things can be true at once. Yes, people are treated differently based on appearance. And yes, a culture that tells everyone to optimize their face, body, skin, hair, weight, age, teeth, and style forever can become cruel very quickly. So this is not a session for ranking people, mocking bodies, or pretending there is one correct way to look. It is a discussion about what we can honestly admit about beauty without becoming worse people.

The question sitting over the room

If appearance really changes how the world treats you, is it kinder to say that out loud — or more dangerous?

A few questions already sitting in my head

Is pretty privilege real in a way polite society still does not want to fully admit? When does self-improvement become empowerment, and when does it become surrendering to a rigged game? Can “just accept yourself” become a way of ignoring the real social cost of being treated as less attractive? Are fitness, skincare, cosmetic procedures, fashion, teeth, hair, and aesthetics part of the same self-improvement system — or are there important ethical lines between them? If future technology makes aesthetic change easier, cheaper, and safer, does that make society more fair or more dystopian? Can we talk honestly about appearance without turning self-worth into a marketplace?

How the discussion will run

We’ll open with the core disagreement: Is this kind of conversation brutal honesty about a real social hierarchy, or does it give too much power to a system we should be resisting?

From there, we’ll move through three questions: How much do looks shape dating, friendship, confidence, work, and everyday treatment? What should people do with that reality: accept it, fight it, optimize within it, or some messy combination? And if aesthetic culture keeps intensifying — fitness science, skincare, cosmetic procedures, anti-aging tools, body transformation tech — what happens to self-worth, fairness, and human dignity?

This is a debate, but not a cruelty contest.

No rating people. No body-shaming. No turning anyone’s appearance into evidence. We are talking about systems, incentives, culture, and lived experience — not putting anyone in the room on trial.

🧠⚠️ What should AI never be allowed to do for us? - Magnifica Humanitas

Interfaith / philosophy discussion - reading packet provided.

Short summary

Most AI debates get boring fast. One side says: relax, it’s just a tool. The other side says: panic, the machines are coming. Too easy. The better question is more uncomfortable: What should AI never be allowed to do for us - even if it can do it efficiently? Care for the lonely? Teach children? Choose who gets hired? Write our apologies? Mediate our friendships? Decide who is risky, useful, visible, employable, or disposable? That is where Magnifica Humanitas gets interesting. The document is not saying “AI is evil.” It is also not saying “AI is neutral.” It asks whether we are building technologies that serve human beings, or systems that quietly redesign human beings into things that are easier to measure, rank, predict, manage, and discard. That is a much better conversation than “AI good / AI bad.”

And to be very clear: this is not a Catholic-only event. Religious people, spiritual people, agnostics, atheists, skeptics, tech people, non-tech people - all welcome. The point is not conversion. The point is not a sermon. The point is not “the Vatican has all the answers.” The point is asking whether secular tech culture is missing something important when it talks about human value only through productivity, convenience, intelligence, scale, and output. Because maybe the most dangerous AI question is not: “Can it think?” Maybe it is: “What kind of human beings are we becoming around it?”

A few questions already sitting in my head

*“What is one human thing you would not want automated, even if a machine could do it efficiently?”

• “When does help become replacement?”

*“Can AI imitate care so well that people stop expecting real care from each other?”

• “Is dignity just a religious word, or do non-religious people need it too?”

*“What happens when a system treats you as a profile, risk score, output, or data trail instead of a person?”

• “What hidden suffering are we willing to ignore because digital life is convenient?”

*“Does AI make us more creative, or more dependent on ready-made answers?”

• “What kind of weakness should be protected instead of upgraded away?”

*“If AI reveals what a society loves, what does our society seem to love most: truth, profit, speed, control, comfort, or real human relationship?”

How the afternoon will go We’ll start with one question: “What is one way AI or algorithms already shape your daily life without asking permission?” Then I’ll give a short reset on the reading packet: Babel vs Jerusalem. Dignity before efficiency. AI as tool, not person. Human beings as more than data, labour, output, or performance. The common good. Hidden costs. What it might mean to stay human. After that, we open the room. Not a tech conference. Not a church event. Not culture-war sludge. Not everyone turning their worldview into a billboard. A serious room, but not a stiff one. Come ready to disagree carefully.

🏡💛 Won’t You Be My Neighbor? - can public kindness exist without becoming sentimental?

Documentary discussion - watch beforehand. Open spoilers.

Short summary

Kindness is one of those words that gets ruined by bad posters. Be kind. Choose kindness. Kindness matters. Fine. True. Also often completely dead on arrival. That is why Won’t You Be My Neighbor? is worth a room. Morgan Neville’s documentary about Fred Rogers is not interesting because it says “kindness is good.” That would be too easy. It is interesting because it shows a person trying to make gentleness serious in a culture that often treats gentleness as weakness, performance, or children’s programming. And somehow that feels more radical now, not less. This is a film about attention, childhood, television, public life, moral imagination, and whether a person can speak softly without becoming naïve. I don’t want a sentimental nostalgia bath. I want the harder conversation: what kind of public kindness is real, what kind is fake, and why modern life seems so bad at telling the difference.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “Why does Fred Rogers feel so unusual now?”
• “Is his kindness simple, or is it actually disciplined?”
• “When does public goodness become sentimental performance?”
• “What did he understand about children that adults still avoid understanding about themselves?”
• “Can gentleness survive in a culture built around irony, speed, and attention-hunger?”
• “Did the documentary make you trust him more, or make you suspicious of your own cynicism?”
• “What would a grown-up version of neighbourliness look like now?”

How the morning will go

Come having watched the documentary beforehand. We’ll start with one question: “What moment felt least sentimental and most real?” Then we’ll stay close to the film: Fred Rogers, television, childhood, public kindness, emotional honesty, religion without salesmanship, and why softness can sometimes be more demanding than toughness. Open spoilers are fine. Not therapy. Not nostalgia worship. Not everyone pretending they are nicer than they are. A real conversation about whether kindness can still have moral weight without turning into wallpaper.

🤝📜 Cicero’s On Friendship - do we love our friends, or what they give us?

Short philosophy reading and discussion - read beforehand.

Short summary

Friendship is one of those words people use warmly and examine very badly. We say “my friends.” We say “community.” We say “chosen family.” We say “I’ve got people.” But what do we actually mean? Cicero’s On Friendship is old, but the question inside it is still awkwardly alive: Do we love our friends for who they are, or for what they give us? Comfort. Status. Access. Validation. Entertainment. A version of ourselves we like being around. Cicero is not writing a modern self-help essay about “finding your people.” He is asking what friendship is supposed to be when it is serious: loyalty, virtue, honesty, usefulness, affection, moral pressure, and whether a good friend should make your life easier or make you better. That’s why this one feels worth a room. Not networking. Not sentimental friendship talk. Not everyone pretending they are a perfect friend. A real conversation about what friendship is, what it costs, and how much of what we call friendship is just mutual convenience with better branding.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “Do we love our friends, or the version of ourselves we get to be around them?”
• “Can a friendship survive if it stops being useful?”
• “Should a real friend make you feel accepted, or tell you when you are becoming worse?”
• “Is loyalty still a virtue if your friend is wrong?”
• “What makes adult friendship so hard to maintain?”
• “Do we choose friends by character, chemistry, shared habits, or shared illusions?”
• “When does friendship become dependency?”

🐦⬜ The Story of a White Blackbird - what happens when being different becomes your entire identity?

Short story reading and discussion - read beforehand.

Short summary

Being different sounds glamorous until it becomes the only thing people can see. Or worse: the only thing you know how to be. Alfred de Musset’s The Story of a White Blackbird is a short, strange little fable from 1842 about difference, vanity, loneliness, recognition, and the trap of turning your outsider status into a whole personality. That is why this one feels weirdly modern. We live in a time where everyone is told to be unique, brandable, legible, interesting, exceptional, somehow unlike the others. But what happens when being different stops being freedom and becomes another cage? The story is short, but the question is not. Do we want to be understood, or admired? Do we want belonging, or proof that we are special? And what happens when identity becomes something we perform so well that we forget whether it was ever real? Not a children’s fable night. Not moral-of-the-story homework. A real conversation about difference, ego, loneliness, and the ugly little hunger to be seen.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “When does being different become a gift, and when does it become a trap?”
• “Do people want to be loved for who they are, or recognized for what makes them unusual?”
• “Can outsider identity become its own kind of vanity?”
• “What happens when you build your whole self around not being like everyone else?”
• “Is it worse to be misunderstood, or to be understood only as ‘the different one’?”
• “How much of modern identity is self-knowledge, and how much is performance?”
• “What would this story look like now, in the age of personal branding and social media?”

How the afternoon will go

We’ll start with one question: “What is one difference people praise in public but punish in real life?” Then we’ll stay close to the story: the fable shape, the comedy, the loneliness, the desire to be seen, and the uneasy line between selfhood and self-display. Not literature-class voice. Not everyone pretending they are above vanity. Not vague identity talk. A real discussion.

Short summary

Summer is not always peaceful. Sometimes it makes people more restless. Heat. Late light. Open windows. City noise. Bodies outside. We’ll meet at Fionn MacCool’s, settle in, pick the question together, and spend the evening arguing properly. Not aggressively. Not academically. Properly. Biography / life-writing discussion - finish the full book beforehand.

Short summary

Some biographies turn people into saints. Some turn them into villains. The better ones make that impossible. Walter Isaacson’s Steve Jobs is useful because Jobs is not easy to flatten. He is brilliant, difficult, obsessive, charismatic, cruel, visionary, controlling, childish, disciplined, impossible, and genuinely consequential. That is exactly why this is worth a room. Not because we need another “genius founder” worship session. Not because everyone should pretend being awful is just the price of greatness. Not because Apple nostalgia needs two hours of our lives. I want the more interesting conversation: What do we do with people who make beautiful things and damage people along the way? How much bad behaviour gets excused when the products are good enough? And why are modern people still so hungry for the myth of the singular genius who bends the world to his taste?

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “Is Jobs admirable, unbearable, or both?”
• “When does intensity become vision, and when is it just cruelty with better branding?”
• “Do great products make people forgive too much?”
• “Was Jobs a genius because he saw what people wanted, or because he forced people to want what he saw?”
• “What does the book reveal about taste as power?”
• “Can someone be a great builder and a bad model for how to live?”
• “Why do we keep wanting business figures to become moral heroes?”
• “What did the biography make you respect more, and what did it make harder to excuse?”

How the afternoon will go

Come having finished the full biography. We’ll start with one question: “What part of Jobs’ life made you most uncomfortable to admire?” Then we’ll stay close to the book: the personality, the work, the relationships, the myth-making, the cruelty, the taste, the ambition, and the way Isaacson turns a business life into a study of character. Full-book spoilers are expected. Not startup worship. Not anti-tech ranting. Not everyone using Jobs as a personality test. A real discussion about life-writing, power, creativity, and the cost of getting exactly what you want.

events.description:
Russian short story reading and discussion - read beforehand.

Short summary

A rich banker and a young lawyer make a stupid argument. Then they turn it into a bet. Fifteen years of isolation. Books, silence, pride, money, boredom, philosophy, rage, religion, literature, and the slow question of whether a person can read enough, think enough, suffer enough, and finally stop wanting what the world keeps selling. That is why Chekhov’s The Bet is such a clean little trap. At first, it looks like a story about capital punishment, prison, money, and intellectual endurance. Then it becomes something stranger: What happens when a person consumes the whole human inheritance - novels, histories, philosophies, sacred texts, languages, music, knowledge - and comes out the other side disgusted by ordinary ambition? Is that wisdom? Or is that just another kind of death? Not Russian-lit intimidation. Not book-report voice. Not everyone pretending they are above money, comfort, attention, or status. A real conversation about what the world offers, what books can change, and whether rejecting everything is enlightenment or collapse.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “Can reading actually transform a person, or just make them better at despising the world?”
• “Is the lawyer wise by the end, broken, arrogant, spiritually free, or some ugly mix?”
• “What does the banker reveal about fear, money, and status?”
• “Would you rather have worldly success and stay shallow, or see through everything and lose your appetite for life?”
• “Is isolation clarifying, or does it make the mind turn against reality?”
• “What kind of knowledge makes people more human, and what kind makes them cold?”
• “If someone gave up money, pleasure, ambition, and public life, would you admire them or worry about them?”

How the morning will go

We’ll start with one question: “What is one thing the world wants you to want?” Then we’ll stay close to the story: the bet, the isolation, the books, the years passing, the banker’s fear, the lawyer’s transformation, and the brutal little ending. events.description:
Science fiction book club discussion - read beforehand.

Short summary

Some science fiction is loud because it wants to impress you. Rendezvous with Rama is quieter than that. A mysterious object enters the solar system. Humans go to look. And the real tension is not just “what is it?” but whether human beings are even capable of encountering something vast without immediately trying to explain, possess, classify, or shrink it down to our size. That is what makes this one worth a room. This is not sci-fi as lore dump. Not space opera noise. Not a fandom room where everyone tries to prove they know the most background detail. A real discussion about awe, mystery, exploration, intelligence, humility, and what happens when the universe refuses to make itself emotionally convenient for us. Some books give you answers. This one is more interested in what happens when the answer stays bigger than the people asking.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “What does the book do with mystery that modern sci-fi often ruins by over-explaining?”
• “Is Rama terrifying, beautiful, indifferent, or all of those at once?”
• “Do the human characters feel small in a good way, or almost too small?”
• “What would actually count as intelligence if it did not care about communicating with us?”
• “Does exploration require humility, or does it always carry some arrogance?”
• “Is the book emotionally cold, or is that part of its power?”
• “What is more unsettling: finding meaning, or finding something that does not need us at all?”

How the morning will go

Come having read the book beforehand. We’ll start with one question: “What image or idea from the book made you feel smallest?” Then we’ll stay close to the book: Rama, the encounter, the mystery, the scale, the human response, and the strange feeling of meeting something that does not exist to satisfy human curiosity. Full-book spoilers are expected. No lore-flexing. No plot-summary sludge. No turning the room into a technical manual. A real science fiction discussion.

events.description:
Reading and discussion night - bring one short passage.

Short summary

You do not need to read a whole book for this one. You just need one paragraph. One passage. One poem stanza. One short excerpt. One bit of language that feels worth putting in front of a room. It can come from a novel, essay, poem, article, speech, memoir, play, letter, weird old book, sharp modern piece, whatever. The only real requirement is that it has something alive inside it. A sentence that bothers you. A paragraph that explains people too well. A line that sounds beautiful but maybe says something ugly. An idea worth arguing with instead of just admiring politely. This is basically a book club without the fake homework. Not open mic energy. Not literature-class stiffness. Not everyone trying to prove they have excellent taste. Just one passage at a time, read closely by people who still think language can do damage.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “What made this passage worth bringing into a room?”
• “Is it beautiful, true, annoying, manipulative, or all of those at once?”
• “What does the writer notice that most people miss?”
• “What word or sentence is doing the most work?”
• “Does this passage actually say something, or does it just sound good?”
• “What did it make you feel before you understood why?”
• “Would this passage survive being argued with?”

Each person brings one short passage. You can read it aloud, say why you brought it, and then we’ll talk about it for a few minutes. Keep it short enough that people can actually hear it and respond. events.description:
Outdoor birdwatching and nature outing - relaxed social walk, not a serious hike.

Short summary

Some outdoor meetups are really just fitness events wearing a nature costume. This is not that. We’re going to George C. Reifel Migratory Bird Sanctuary for a slow birdwatching / nature walk through wetlands and marshes. Quiet trails. Water. Birds doing strange bird things. People talking softly instead of performing personality at full volume. This is a relaxed Curiosity Club outing, not a serious hike and not an expert birding event. You do not need to know bird names. You do not need fancy gear. You just need to be willing to slow down, look carefully, and not make the ducks regret civilization.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “Why does watching birds make people quieter in a good way?”
• “What changes when the point of a walk is noticing, not arriving?”
• “Do we go into nature to escape the city, or to remember how overstimulated we’ve become?”
• “What animal behaviour feels weirdly human once you actually watch it?”
• “When was the last time you stood still long enough for something to appear?”

How the afternoon will go

We’ll meet at the sanctuary entrance at 2:00 PM. From there, we’ll walk the trails together at an easy pace, stop when something interesting appears, and keep the afternoon social but calm. Most visits take about 1 to 1.5 hours, and the sanctuary closes at 4:00 PM, so everyone needs to be out by then. No rush. No route-maximizing. No turning birdwatching into a competition. Just a slow afternoon outside with decent people and better-than-usual reasons to look around.

Reservations / admission

Science fiction book club discussion - read beforehand.

Short summary

Some science fiction is loud because it wants to impress you. Rendezvous with Rama is quieter than that. A mysterious object enters the solar system. Humans go to look. And the real tension is not just “what is it?” but whether human beings are even capable of encountering something vast without immediately trying to explain, possess, classify, or shrink it down to our size. That is what makes this one worth a room. This is not sci-fi as lore dump. Not space opera noise. Not a fandom room where everyone tries to prove they know the most background detail. A real discussion about awe, mystery, exploration, intelligence, humility, and what happens when the universe refuses to make itself emotionally convenient for us. Some books give you answers. This one is more interested in what happens when the answer stays bigger than the people asking.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “What does the book do with mystery that modern sci-fi often ruins by over-explaining?”
• “Is Rama terrifying, beautiful, indifferent, or all of those at once?”
• “Do the human characters feel small in a good way, or almost too small?”
• “What would actually count as intelligence if it did not care about communicating with us?”
• “Does exploration require humility, or does it always carry some arrogance?”
• “Is the book emotionally cold, or is that part of its power?”
• “What is more unsettling: finding meaning, or finding something that does not need us at all?”

How the morning will go

Come having read the book beforehand. We’ll start with one question: “What image or idea from the book made you feel smallest?” Then we’ll stay close to the book: Rama, the encounter, the mystery, the scale, the human response, and the strange feeling of meeting something that does not exist to satisfy human curiosity. Full-book spoilers are expected. No lore-flexing. No plot-summary sludge. No turning the room into a technical manual. A real science fiction discussion.

Short Summary

This is designed for those with little to no knowledge of Canadian banking and investing. It will cover the basics of bank account types, investing methods, tax advantages, and how they all relate to each other. The goal is to equip you with a solid understanding of the core concepts.

** IMPORTANT **

This is not a product or service and does not involve any sales, cost, or subscription. You will not be asked for anything other than to listen, to ask questions if you need something clarified, and to be respectful of others.

Who am I?

My name is Cezary. Over the past 2 decades I learned how money works in Canada and how to invest it. I have now reached my financial goals and am sharing what I have learned to help others get started.

Who is this for?

You are ready to start learning about banking and investing, but feel overwhelmed at all the information out there and are looking to understand the foundational basics first.

What will we cover?

We will cover the structure of the Canadian banking system (not deep, just enough to help with everything else) and dive into the following:

• Account types (CHQ / SAV, RRSP, TFSA, FHSA, RESP, etc)
• Different holdings (cash, good / bad debt, GIC, HYSA, Mutual Funds, ETFs, Stocks / Bonds)
• How the above relate to each other and which to use first to reach your goals
• Investment methods and risk tolerance
• Tax advantages and strategies
• Common ways to invest (Managed investing vs Self-directed vs Robo-investing)
• Examples of how to get started at a major bank or brokerage
• Additional resources you can use to continue your learning journey

The session is designed to take \~30 minutes, but I encourage questions during the presentation so expect us to take 45 - 60 minutes to cover everything. If you have questions on any topic too advanced for this BASICS session, I’m happy to answer them after the session.

What should you bring / prepare?

• Pen and paper - You will create one chart and take notes as needed
• Questions you’d like answered - I’m happy to answer in front of the whole group or privately

This is a fun, casual Sunday night at Fionn MacCool’s for people who want music, food, drinks, laughter, and cheering each other on! You do not need to be a good singer. Outdoor beach ritual and social - adults only, 18+.

Short summary

Late summer is upon us! A season turning the corner while everyone begins to ponder about what comes next. This is a relaxed Jericho Beach gathering with a more intentional centre: a beach social arrival, then a simple threshold ritual around release, reset, and choosing what we want to carry forward. Not a full moon event. Not a party. Not therapy. Not professional meditation instruction. Just a small ritual of positivity and possibility on the beach; oracle cards, a meaningful object if you want to bring one, breathwork and meditation, journaling, writing down something to release, and a symbolic non-fire release. No burning paper. No open fire. We’ll keep it grounded: write what you’re releasing, tear the paper, and carry every scrap out with you. The beach gives us so much, it does not need our litter.

How the evening will go

We’ll start with a relaxed beach arrival so people can settle, talk, eat, and get comfortable. Then we’ll move into the intentional part of the evening: oracle-card reading, a short breathwork or meditation moment, journaling, writing down something to release, and a symbolic release ritual without fire. Bring crystals, oracle cards, or another meaningful personal object if that fits you. Or bring nothing mystical at all and just come with paper, a pen, and a little honesty. Belief is welcome. Skepticism is welcome. Performative spirituality is not required.

Important beach note

Jericho Beach is a public, family-friendly beach. Everyone attending through this Meetup should remain in regular beach clothing or swimwear for the whole event. Adults only, 18+. Be respectful, calm, and normal about sharing a public beach.

Bring

Paper and pen. Blanket, mat, or towel. Warm evening layers. Your own snacks and drinks. Optional swimsuit. Optional oracle cards. Optional crystals or another meaningful personal object.

Practical notes

This ritual will not involve actual fire or burning paper. We’ll use a symbolic non-fire release instead. If we tear paper as part of the release, every scrap comes back out with us. This is an outdoor beach event, so dress for the evening and the weather.

🗓️ Date: Saturday, August 15th, 2026 🕒 Time: 7:00 PM - 10:00 PM 📍 Location: Jericho Beach Jericho Beach Pier, 1300 Discovery St, Vancouver, BC Meeting point: We’ll meet at the Jericho Beach Pier map pin at 1300 Discovery St. I’ll post the exact gathering spot in the event comments before the event.

Cap

No attendee cap for this one. Come with grounded energy, respect for the beach, and something you are ready to release without making it everyone else’s problem.

Video discussion - watch beforehand. No screening.

Short summary

Elon Musk is almost impossible to discuss normally. Some people treat him like a prophet. Some people treat him like a cartoon villain. Both versions are lazy. This discussion is built around The Economist’s full-length interview with Elon Musk, which runs about 85 minutes and gives us a lot to work with: AI, power, politics, Starlink, Ukraine, China, Sam Altman, work becoming optional, Musk’s conflicts with other AI leaders, and the much bigger question underneath all of it: Should one person have this much influence over the future? That is the room I want. Not fanboy worship. Not dunking for two hours. Not everyone arriving with their take already laminated. A real discussion about technology, power, ego, accountability, AI risk, politics, and what happens when private individuals start operating at the scale of states.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “Is Musk mostly a builder, a chaos agent, a political actor, or all three?”
• “If AI becomes smarter than humans within five years, who should be trusted to shape that transition?”
• “Can AI companies regulate themselves, or is that basically asking power to politely limit itself?”
• “Should one person have this much control over infrastructure, communication, satellites, companies, and public narratives?”
• “Does Musk’s political involvement make his technological power more dangerous, or just more visible?”
• “What do people misunderstand about Musk because they either love him or hate him too quickly?”
• “If work becomes optional, is that liberation, fantasy, or a problem we are not emotionally ready for?”
• “When does visionary ambition become too much power in one person’s hands?”

How the morning will go

Come having watched the interview beforehand. We’ll start with one question: “What is the strongest version of the case for taking Musk seriously - and the strongest version of the case for being worried?” Then we’ll stay close to the interview: AI timelines, China, self-regulation, Musk’s conflicts with Sam Altman and other AI leaders, Starlink and Ukraine, USAID claims, Europe, the far right, Britain, racism accusations, and the question of what people misunderstand about him. 🔥🚁 Apocalypse Now - war, madness, spectacle, and the end of command

Movie discussion - watch beforehand. No screening.

Short summary

Some movies are about war. Apocalypse Now feels more like war having a fever dream about itself. It is huge, beautiful, obscene, hypnotic, ridiculous, and rotten in a way that still makes most modern war movies look too clean. This is not just a Vietnam film. It is about command breaking down, spectacle replacing meaning, violence turning mystical, men losing the ability to tell the difference between mission and madness. That is why it still deserves a room. Not because it is “important cinema.” Because it is still disturbing. A movie this visually powerful should make us suspicious of our own attention.

A few questions already sitting in my head

• “Is the movie condemning spectacle, or seducing us with it?”
• “At what point does the mission stop making sense?”
• “Is Kurtz insane, honest, monstrous, or just what the war was already becoming?”
• “What does the film understand about command and masculinity?”
• “Which scene felt most impossible to forget?”
• “Does the movie have a moral center, or is that exactly what has collapsed?”

How the afternoon will go

Come having watched the film beforehand. We’ll start with one question: “What scene still feels lodged in your nervous system?” Then we’ll stay close to the film: Willard, Kurtz, the river, the helicopters, the spectacle, the horror, and the feeling that order has become a costume. Not trivia. Not film-bro monologues. Not war-movie ranking night. A real discussion.

🌙📓 Late-night Journaling - weekly reflection hour

Weekly reflection and journaling gathering at a coffee shop.

Short summary

Some weeks disappear without ever being looked at. You work. You scroll. You answer messages. You carry things around in your head like they are going to organize themselves out of politeness. They don’t. This is a simple one-hour journaling meetup at Trees Organic Coffee: a small weekly container to slow down, reflect on the week, and write independently for a while. Nothing dramatic. No big circle of emotional speeches. No pressure to share your writing. No pretending your notebook is about to fix your entire life. Just one quiet hour, a table, a notebook, and a few people choosing to actually show up for a slower Sunday evening.

How the hour will go

We’ll meet at the back of the coffee shop on the long tables. The format is simple: arrive, settle in, write, reflect, and let the week land on paper. You can write about your week, what you avoided, what helped, what drained you, what you want to carry forward, or whatever your mind keeps circling. Nobody has to share their writing. This is not a Silent Reading Party. This is not a Meditation + Journaling Circle. This is not therapy. It is quieter and simpler than that. Please only RSVP if you genuinely plan to come. The room works better when the people on the list actually show up, even if it is a small group.

Bring

Notebook and pen. Buying something from the coffee shop is optional, but encouraged.

When and where

🗓️ Date: Sunday, August 16th, 2026 🕒 Time: 6:00 PM - 7:00 PM 📍 Location: Trees Organic Coffee 738 Granville Street, Vancouver, BC Meeting point: at the back of the coffee shop on the long tables. Cap: 10 Small on purpose so it stays calm and real.

A quieter middle of the week

By Wednesday, most people are already carrying a little too much. Messages, errands, work thoughts, unfinished conversations, the weird background noise of the week. This is a warm midweek reset: a small room at the library where we slow down together, sit with a short reading, meditate, write, and have a real but gentle conversation before heading back into the rest of the week. 🌙 You can come solo. Most people do. The room is meant to feel welcoming and social without turning into a mixer.

What we’ll do

This is the Wednesday companion to the Tuesday Contemplative Meditation + Journaling Circle. We’ll use the same session material and the same reading as Tuesday. The session includes short opening comments, a short reading, contemplative meditation, a brief pass-the-stick reflection, journaling, and open discussion. It is not guided visualization. No meditation or journaling experience is needed.

The feel of the room

You do not need to say something profound. You do not need to share your writing. You just need to arrive with enough willingness to sit, listen, write, and let the room settle around you. Please arrive on time so we can begin together. This kind of room works best when people settle in at the same time.

Bring

Notebook and pen. ✍️ Optional: water or tea, sweater, cushion, or anything that helps you sit comfortably. This is not therapy or professional meditation instruction - just a simple shared practice for attention, reflection, and a little more honesty than the week usually allows.

When and where

🗓️ Date: Wednesday, August 12th, 2026 🕒 Time: 6:00 PM - 8:00 PM 📍 Location: Vancouver Central Library 350 West Georgia Street, Vancouver, BC Level 4, Room 492 South Capacity: 12 + waitlist.
